column2: Then the Pandava's bowstring, drawn too hard, suddenly snapped with a loud sound; at that moment the charioteer's son covered Partha with a hundred small arrows.
With sharp arrows like serpents freed from their skins, washed in oil, bird-feathered, he pierced Vasudeva with sixty iron arrows; meanwhile the Somakas fled.

Then quickly restringing his bow and dispelling the arrows loosed by Adhiratha's son, Partha, enraged, his limbs wounded by Karna's arrows, confronted the Somakas in the battle; no birds flew in the sky, a darkness having been made by his swift weapon.
Partha, laughing, pierced Shalya hard in the armour with ten arrows; then, piercing Karna with twelve well-loosed ones, he pierced him again with seven.
Deeply struck by feathered arrows of fierce speed, driven with the force of Partha's bow, with limbs pierced and body smeared with blood, Karna shone like Rudra with bow drawn.
Then Adhiratha's son pierced Dhananjaya, equal to the lord of the three ten-regions, with three arrows, and sent five blazing arrows like serpents at Achyuta, wishing to kill him.
Piercing the best man's armour, they fell, well loosed, in gold-painted fashion, entering the earth with force, bathed there, and turned again towards Karna.
Dhananjaya quickly cut each of those five into three with swiftly loosed broad-headed arrows; they fell to earth, like the feathers of the great-horse Takshaka's son.

Then Kiriti blazed, burning as fire burns dry grass in anger; with arrows drawn to the ear and loosed, blazing, ending bodies, he pierced Karna in his vitals; Karna swayed in pain, but stood, of exceeding fortitude.
Then, O king, with floods of arrows the quarters and intermediate quarters, and Karna's sun-bright chariot, became invisible when Dhananjaya was angered, like the sky covered with frost and fog.
Then those who protected the wheels and feet and the leaders and rear-guards, all slayers of foes approved by Duryodhana, gathered, fine chariot-warriors, the essence of the army—
two thousand of the Kuru heroes, bulls among the Kurus, Savyasachin alone in a moment brought to destruction, with their chariots, horses and charioteers, O king.
Then your sons and the remaining Kurus fled, abandoning Karna, scattering over their slain and those wounded by arrows, lamenting sons and fathers.
Seeing all quarters empty, bereft of the Kurus scattered by fear, Karna was not pained there, O Bharata, and ran straight at Arjuna.
That weapon of Arjuna's swallowed heroes, and the sky resounded without end; loosed by enraged Partha then quickly for Karna's slaying, in the great crush.
By the Atharvana weapon, of great majesty, destroyer of foes, obtained from Rama, Karna destroyed that burning weapon of Arjuna and struck Partha with sharp arrows.
Then a very great crush took place of Arjuna and Adhiratha's son, O king, as they struck each other with arrows, like two elephants with the blows of their tusks.
Then Karna fixed a foe-slaying, well-sharpened, serpent-mouthed, blazing, dreadful arrow, well washed, long kept in battle for Partha,
always worshipped, lying in sandal-powder, resting in a golden tube, of great poison, blazing, born of Airavata's line, wishing to take Phalguna's head in the battle.
The great-souled king of the Madras said to him, seeing Vaikartana with the arrow aimed: "This arrow will not reach Karna's neck; take aim and fix an arrow that kills at the head."
Then Karna, his eyes red with rage, with the arrow fixed, said forcibly to Shalya: "Karna does not fix an arrow twice, Shalya; those like me are not given to deceit."
Having so spoken, he loosed that arrow, honoured like a cloud heavy with rain; saying "You are slain, Phalguna!", he quickly loosed the mighty one.
Then the charioteer's son, with his arrow, in his best effort, anger and exertion, took off Arjuna's crown, ornament of his head, renowned in earth, sky, heaven and waters.
That crown, adorned with a net of gold, pearls and jewels, bright as sun, moon, fire and planets, made by the Self-existent himself by austerity and effort for Purandara,
of great worth, causing fear to foes, shining exceedingly, pleasant and fragrant, which the lord of the gods himself gladly gave to Kiritin when he had slain the enemies of the gods,

which the gods themselves, even the best, could not harm, not by Hara, Varuna, Indra or Kubera, with Pinaka, noose, thunderbolt and the best of arrows—that Vrisha (Karna) forcibly took with the serpent.
Churned by that best of arrows with poison and fire, blazing, radiant, dear to the earth, the excellent crown of Partha fell, like the sun blazing as it falls from the mountain of setting.
Then the serpent by force took from Arjuna's head the crown set with many jewels, as Mahendra's thunderbolt takes the finest peak of a mountain with flowering trees and fresh sprouts.
Earth, sky and heaven and the waters were shaken by the wind, O Bharata, as if split; so a sound arose in the worlds, and people grew uncertain, pained and stumbled.
Then, tying up his own hair with a white cloth, Arjuna stood pained in head and knees, shining as the rising mountain with the sun on its peak, its rays complete.
The clouds, set going by Karna's arm, then a great serpent bright as fire and sun, having an enmity with Arjuna, rose up after reaching the crown.
It said to him: "Know me, Krishna, as the one who has offended; I bear the enmity born of my mother's slaying." Then Krishna said to Partha in battle, "Slay the great serpent who has made enmity."
Thus addressed by Madhusudana, the Gandiva-bowman, fierce-bowed against foes, said, "Who is this serpent that came himself into Garuda's mouth?"
[Krishna said:] "He who, when you satisfied Chitrabhanu (Agni) at Khandava with this bow, went into the sky, his body cut by arrows, many-formed—his mother was slain by you."
Then Jishnu, sparing the rest, cut with six sharp, well-edged arrows that serpent as he flew in a slanting course in the sky; his limbs cut, he fell to the earth.
At that moment Karna pierced the hero among men, Dhananjaya, as he looked askance, with ten stone-whetted peacock-feathered arrows.
Then Arjuna, piercing with twelve sharp arrows loosed to the ear, loosed an iron arrow of speed equal to a venomous serpent, drawn full to the ear.
It split that finest of variegated armours, as if taking away his life, well loosed, and drinking Karna's blood entered the earth, smeared with blood.
Then Vrisha, enraged by the fall of the arrow, like a great serpent struck with a rod, quickly loosed the best of arrows, like a very venomous serpent its deadliest venom.
He pierced Janardana with twelve and Arjuna with ninety-nine arrows, and again the Pandava with a dreadful arrow, and Karna roared and laughed.
The Pandava could not bear his joy and pierced his vitals; then, knowing vitals, Indra-valorous Arjuna struck him with feathered arrows, as Indra struck Bala with vigour.
Then Arjuna loosed ninety-nine arrows at Karna, like Death's rod; struck hard by the arrows, with body exerted, he trembled, as a mountain split by a thunderbolt.
His excellent ornament of finest jewels, thunderbolts and gold fell to the ground, cast down by Dhananjaya's arrows, and his excellent earrings too.
His shining excellent armour, made at great expense by the best artisans with effort, over a very long time, the Pandava shattered in a moment by arrows in many ways.
Then, enraged, he pierced him, bereft of armour, with four excellent arrows; he, struck by the foe, was greatly pained, like a patient with wounds from bile, phlegm and wind.
With sharp shafts issuing from the circle of the great bow, loosed with skill, effort and strength, Arjuna swiftly hewed Karna with many of the best arrows and pierced his vitals.
Deeply struck by Partha's fierce-speed feathered arrows of many kinds with sharp points, Karna shone like a mountain red with ochre, streaming blood like water from falls.
Kiriti covered Karna with his horses and chariot with calf-tooth arrows, O Bharata, and filled the quarters with gold-feathered arrows with all effort.
Covered with calf-tooth arrows, broad-chested, he, Adhiratha's son, shone like a mountain with flowering ashoka, palasha and silk-cotton trees, with syandana and sandal.
With arrows lodged in many ways in his body, Karna shone in battle, O lord of men, like Mahendra's mountain with trees on its slopes and caves, with fair karnikara trees.
Loosing masses of arrows from his bow, Karna, with rays of nets of arrows, bloody, with a circle of red rays, shone as the sun facing the setting.
The arrows loosed from Adhiratha's arms like blazing great serpents were destroyed by the arrows loosed from Arjuna's arms, reaching them in all directions with sharp points.
Then his wheel sank into the earth; bewildered in the battle, the charioteer's son, with his chariot reeling from the Brahmana's curse, and his weapon obtained from Rama not appearing,

unable to bear those calamities, shaking his hands, reviling, said: "The knowers of dharma always say that dharma protects those who are devoted to dharma; but today dharma does not protect me, my devotee; I think dharma does not always protect."
Saying so, with his horses and charioteer faltering, shaken by the falls of Arjuna's weapons, faltering in actions because of blows to his vitals, he reviled dharma again and again in the battle.
Then Karna with three most dreadful arrows pierced his hand in battle, and Partha with seven.
Then Arjuna loosed seventeen keen, unswerving arrows, equal to Indra's thunderbolt, dreadful, like fire.
Piercing him, those fierce-speed arrows fell to the ground; Karna, trembling, showed his effort with his dart.
Then, steadying himself by strength, he brought forth the Brahma weapon; and Arjuna, seeing it, invoked the Indra weapon.
Consecrating Gandiva, bowstring and arrows, Dhananjaya loosed showers of arrows, as Purandara rains.
Then arrows made of splendour issued from Partha's chariot and appeared great in valour near Karna's chariot.
The great chariot-warrior made those, before him, ineffective; then, when that weapon was destroyed, the Vrishni hero said:
Loose the supreme weapon, Partha; Radheya swallows your arrows. Arjuna too invoked and applied the Brahma weapon.
Then, delighting with arrows and whirling Karna, Arjuna; enraged, Karna cut his bowstring with sharp arrows.
Then the Pandava, fixing another string and wiping it, covered Karna by thousands with blazing arrows.
Karna did not notice the cutting of his string nor the stringing of it in the battle, because of the swiftness; it was as if marvellous.
Radheya countered Savyasachin's weapons with weapons and displayed his own valour superior to Partha's.
Then Krishna, seeing Arjuna tormented by Karna's weapon, said to Partha, "Resort to the unsurpassed weapon; repeat it."
Then Dhananjaya, consecrating another divine arrow, fiery, like snake poison, made of stone-essence,
took the dreadful weapon, wishing to hurl it, Kiritin; then the earth swallowed Radheya's wheel in the great battle.
His wheel swallowed, Radheya shed tears of anger; he said to Arjuna also, "Wait a moment, Pandava.
Seeing my wheel swallowed in the middle by fate, Partha, avoid this resolve practised by the base.
One with dishevelled hair, turned away, a Brahmana, with joined palms, who has sought refuge, laid down weapons, or fallen into calamity, Arjuna,
one without arrows, with armour fallen, with weapons broken and fallen—heroes do not strike such in battle, nor do kings; and you are a hero, Kaunteya; therefore wait a moment.
Until I lift this wheel from the earth, Dhananjaya, you ought not to strike me on the ground while you are in your chariot, Pandava; I do not fear Vasudeva or you.
For you are a kshatriya's heir, increaser of a great family; remembering the teaching of dharma, wait a moment, Pandava."
[Krishna said:] "When you brought Draupadi in one garment into the assembly, you and Suyodhana, Duhshasana, and Shakuni son of Subala, where was your dharma then, Karna?
When in the assembly Shakuni, skilled in dice, conquered Yudhishthira, son of Kunti, who was unskilled in dice, where had your dharma gone?
When Draupadi, in her season, was in Duhshasana's power in the assembly, you laughed, Karna; where had your dharma gone then?
Greedy for the kingdom, Karna, you challenged the Pandava again, relying on the king of Gandhara; where had your dharma gone then?"
When Vasudeva had thus spoken to Radheya, a fierce anger entered the Pandava, Dhananjaya, remembering this and that.
From his anger, flames of splendour issued from all his pores, O great king; it was as marvellous.
Seeing him, Karna rained the Brahma weapon on Dhananjaya and again made effort to raise his chariot; the Pandava warded off that weapon with a weapon and struck him.
Then the son of Kunti loosed at Karna another weapon, dear to Fire; it blazed exceedingly.
Karna quenched the fire with the Varuna weapon and made all quarters dark and gloomy with clouds.
The valiant Pandava, unflurried, with the Vayavya weapon swept away the clouds in Radheya's sight.

And the elephant-rope of Karna's best banner, with arrows, burnished with gold, pearls, jewels and diamonds, made by the finest artisans with the greatest effort over time, finely shaped and lofty, dispelling darkness—
always the producer of vigour for your army, frightening foes, praiseworthy in form, renowned in the world as equal to the sun, in splendour equal to fire, sun and moon—
then Kiriti, the great soul, struck down with a sharp gold-feathered razor-arrow, exerting himself, the blazing banner of the great chariot-warrior, Adhiratha's son.
With that banner fell, O revered one, fame, dharma, victory and all that was dear; hearts of the Kurus fell and a great cry of "Alas" arose.
Then, in haste for Karna's slaying, Partha took from his quiver an anjalika arrow like Mahendra's thunderbolt, fire and Death's rod, like the best ray of the thousand-rayed sun,
piercing vitals, smeared with blood and flesh, radiant as the fire and sun, of great worth, taker of men, horses and elephants, three cubits long, six-feathered, of fierce speed;
equal in splendour to the thousand-eyed one's thunderbolt, unbearable like a flesh-eater, resembling Pinaka and Narayana's discus, terrifying, destroyer of the living.

Joining it with the supreme great weapon and its mantra, drawing Gandiva, he said with a roar: "This great incomparable weapon-arrow I bear, which pierces the body and swiftly takes the life of a foe.
If I have performed austerity, pleased my elders, and heard and done the wish of my friends, by that truth let this arrow slay Karna, my foe, well armoured and unconquered."
Having said so, Dhananjaya loosed the dreadful arrow for Karna's slaying, like the fierce Atharvangirasa sorcery, blazing, unbearable in battle even by Death.
Saying, Kiriti, greatly delighted: "May this arrow of mine bring victory, wishing to kill one equal to sun and moon in power, may it lead Karna to his end for Yama."
With that excellent arrow, bringing victory, delighted, Kiriti, the aggressor, wishing to slay the one equal to sun and moon in splendour, pinned his foe.
That head, shining like the risen sun, like the sun in mid-sky, fell to the ground, the head of the commander, like the red disc of the sun falling to the setting mountain.
His body, long joined with ease to that noble-deeded one's form, left it with great difficulty, as a lord leaves a great wealthy house he is attached to.
Shattered by arrows, bereft of life and armour, Karna's tall body fell, streaming blood from wounds like water of red ochre, like the head of a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
From the body of the fallen Karna a blazing splendour rose and entered the sky; that marvel all the human warriors saw, O king, when Karna was slain.

Seeing him slain and lying there, the Somakas, delighted, raised a cry with their armies, played instruments with great joy, waved their garments and arms, and others, strong, danced, embracing one another, roaring and saying:
Seeing Karna groaning on the ground, felled from his chariot and pierced by an arrow, like a fire cast down by a great wind at the end of a sacrifice, on a couch at the close of night,
his body, covered all over with arrows and drenched in floods of blood, shone like the sun with its own rays.
Having scorched the enemy host with blazing rays of arrows, the sun Karna was led to its setting by the strong time, Arjuna.
As the sun, going to its setting, takes its radiance with it, so Karna's arrow went taking his life.
In the afternoon, O revered one, the head of the charioteer's son, cut off in the battle by an anjalika arrow, fell, lofty.
Over and over the armies, the arrow swiftly carried off the head of that foe, Karna's lofty head.
[Sanjaya said:] Seeing the brave Karna fallen on the earth, covered with arrows, his body smeared with blood, the king of the Madras departed in the chariot with its banner cut.
With Karna slain, the Kurus fled, tormented by fear, deeply wounded in the battle, looking again and again at Arjuna's great banner blazing in its form.
His head, with a face like a thousand-petalled lotus, equal to the thousand-eyed one's deeds, fell to the earth as the thousand-rayed sun at day's end.
Seeing that army with chariots, horses and elephants felled and the charioteer's son slain, Duryodhana, his eyes filled with tears, sighed again and again, in distress.
They stood surrounding the brave Karna fallen on the earth, covered with arrows, his body smeared with blood, wishing to see him, like the sun fallen to earth by chance.
Some were delighted, some terrified, some downcast, some bewildered, and others as if grieved—the enemy and yours—each according to his nature.
Seeing Karna with armour, ornaments, garments and weapons scattered, struck by Dhananjaya, his vigour gone, the Kurus fled, like cows whose bull is slain, in confusion.
After a great crush by Arjuna, seeing Karna slain, like an elephant by a lion, lying on the ground, the king of the Madras, afraid, retreated swiftly with his chariot.
The lord of the Madras, bewildered, quickly in a chariot with its banner removed, came to Duryodhana and, addressing him in his sorrow, said:

Your army, with its elephants, horses and chariot-heroes shattered, like the realm of Yama, has been slain by one another, by great men, horses and elephants like mountain peaks.
mahabharata:8:68.9	Such a battle, Bharata, never was as that of Karna and Arjuna today; the two Krishnas met with Karna and swallowed him, and all your other enemies.
mahabharata:8:68.12	The kings, almost invulnerable, wishing your good, were slain by the Pandavas in battle; so do not grieve, Bharata; this is fate; success comes in turn, success is not always.
mahabharata:8:68.13	Hearing these words of the lord of the Madras and seeing in his mind his own folly, Duryodhana, dejected, senseless, sighed again and again, in distress.
mahabharata:8:68.14	To him, dumb in thought, wretched and greatly afflicted, Artayani (Shalya) said sorrowfully: See this fierce battlefield, hero, filled with slain men, horses and elephants,
with fallen great elephants like mountains, hit once and pierced in the vitals, with those writhing and lifeless, with warriors whose machines, weapons and armour are broken,
as if with mountain-kings hurled by thunderbolts, with split stones, deer, trees and herbs, with bells, goads, javelins and banners thrown down, with golden garlands, soaked in floods of blood,
with horses pierced by arrows and fallen, others gasping and vomiting blood, groaning dismally, with rolling eyes, biting the earth and crying piteously,
with elephants, horses and warriors cast aside, the faintly alive and the lifeless, with men, horses, elephants and chariots crushed, the earth is as hard to see as the great Vaitarani.

Fallen, trembling elephants with severed hands and limbs on the earth, the renowned elephant, chariot, horse and foot warriors slain facing the enemy, with armour, ornaments, garments and weapons scattered, the earth is covered as if with fires at the end of night.

Thousands of mighty men fallen, struck by arrows, watched as they lie, with senses lost, breathing again, the earth became as if followed by fires; the earth, shining fiercely with the fallen from heaven, like the night sky with bright planets.
The arrows loosed from the arms of Karna and Arjuna, piercing the bodies of elephants, horses and men, swiftly took their lives and went into the earth, like great serpents into their dwellings.
With men, horses and elephants slain in the battle, and chariots split by arrows, the path of Dhananjaya and Adhiratha's son was impassable for elephants, the earth very rough.
With chariots, arrows and warriors crushed, charioteers, horses, weapons and banners transfixed, weapons shattered, chariot-seats cut, wheels, axles, yokes and triple poles cut,
with machines released, iron slain, quivers and seats ruined, with nests broken, adorned with jewels and gold, the earth was strewn as if heaven with autumn clouds.
With swift, adorned horses dragged, with well-prepared battle chariots whose lords were slain, crushed in many ways, going rapidly with heaps of men, elephants, chariots and horses,
with golden bands, iron clubs, axes, kadangaras, pestles, pattishas, and spotless drawn swords, maces bound with plates of gold, fell.
Bows, ornaments with golden armlets, arrows with variegated gold feathers, yellow lances, spotless drawn swords, and bright spears with swords.
Parasols, fly-whisks, conches, garlands of the best flowers variegated with gold, blankets, banners wrapped in cloth, diadem-garlands and white crowns.
Scattered whisks, blankets, trembling strings of pearls chief among them, head-ornaments, armlets and fine bracelets, necklaces and gold-threaded medallions,
the finest jewels, diamonds, gold, pearls, and gems of various auspicious kinds, bodies fit for the greatest comfort, and heads with faces like the moon—
leaving their bodies, enjoyments and equipment, and even pleasing comforts, having attained the great devotion to their own duty, they went to worlds filled with fame."
Having said this, Shalya ceased; Duryodhana, his mind overcome with grief, saying "Alas, Karna! Alas, Karna!", distressed, senseless, with eyes full of tears,
the kings led by Drona's son, all consoling him, went with him, looking again and again at Arjuna's great banner blazing with glory.
The earth, sprinkled with blood from the bodies of men, horses and elephants, with red garments and garlands and gold, shone like a woman, accessible to all.
Their forms covered with blood, O king, shining exceedingly at that terrible hour, the Kurus, seeing it, did not remain; all the worlds of the gods were departed.
Greatly grieved at Karna's slaying, saying "Alas, Karna! Alas, Karna!", they went quickly to their camps, O king, looking at the red sun.
With gold-feathered sharp arrows loosed from Gandiva, blood-smeared and feathered, Karna lay on the ground, his limbs covered with arrows, shining though slain, like the sun with its rays.
Karna's body, drenched with blood, the Lord Vivasvat (the sun), compassionate to his devotee, touching it with his rays, red-hued, went to the great ocean to bathe, as it were.
Thus reflecting, the hosts of gods and sages, grouped, went each to his dwelling, and people, reflecting, dispersed at ease, in sky and on earth.
Hearing of that wondrous, fearful-to-the-living battle of the two chief Kuru heroes, Dhananjaya and Adhiratha's son, the people went away astonished, praising.
Even slain, the hero Radheya, whose armour was cut by arrows, lying on his couch of arrows, lifeless, was not abandoned by splendour.
Adorned with ornaments of many kinds, O king, with bright gold armlets, Vaikartana lay slain like a tree with sprouts.
Like the best of gold, as if blazing fire, with his son, the tiger among men was quenched by Partha's splendour; having scorched the Pandavas and Panchalas, O king, with the splendour of his weapons.
He who, begged by good suppliants, always said "I give" and never "I will not"—that good man Vrisha was slain in the duel.
He who gave all to Brahmanas, for himself, and for whom there was nothing not to be given to Brahmanas, even his own life,
ever dear to men, giver, fond of giving, went to heaven, taking away your sons' hope of victory, shelter and armour.
When Karna was slain, rivers did not flow; the sun, turbid, went to its setting; a planet slanting, bright as blazing sun, rose, Yama's son, O king.
The sky split, the earth roared, winds blew harshly beyond measure, the quarters blazed with smoke, and the great oceans surged with a roar.
Mountains with forests and ranges shook, and bands of beings were pained, O revered one; Brihaspati, pressing Rohini, became of colour like moon and sun.
When Karna was slain, the quarters were not distinguished, the sky was covered with darkness, the earth shook, meteors blazing like fire fell, and night-rangers rejoiced.
When Arjuna struck off with a razor-arrow Karna's head, face shining like the moon, then in the sky and on earth repeatedly a cry of "Alas!" of the people arose.
Having slain Karna, his enemy, in the battle, honoured by gods, gandharvas and men, Arjuna Partha shone with supreme splendour, like the thousand-eyed one having slain Vritra.

Then in his chariot, resounding like a mass of clouds, bright as the sun in mid-sky, with a pennant and a fearsome-sounding banner, shining white as snow, moon, conch and crystal, adorned with gold, pearls, jewels, diamonds and coral, of incomparable speed,
the two best of men, the Pandava and the slayer of Keshi, said to be like fire and sun, shone fearless in the battlefield, as Vishnu and Vasava on one vehicle.

Then, with the roar of bowstring, palm and wheel-rims, having by force made their enemies lustreless, having accomplished the Kurus with floods of arrows, the monkey-bannered and the bird-bannered blew their conches of fair sound by force, depressing the hearts of their foes.
Taking in their hands the great-sounding snow-white conches covered with nets of gold, the two best of men kissed their excellent conches and blew them at once with their fair mouths.
The roar of Panchajanya and of Devadatta filled earth, sky, heaven and the waters.
Making the forests, mountains, rivers and quarters resound with the conch-sound, terrifying your son's army, the two heroes gladdened Yudhishthira.
Then the Kurus fled with speed, hearing the sounding of the conches, leaving the lord of the Madras and their lord Duryodhana, O Bharata, of the Bharatas.
Then assembled hosts of beings rejoiced in Dhananjaya, shining greatly in the great battle, and in Janardana, like the two lights risen.
Covered by Karna's arrows, the two scorchers of foes, Achyuta and Arjuna, shone in the battle, having dispelled darkness, like risen spotless moon and sun with garlands of rays.

I am Sanjaya, tiger among men; salutations to you, best of the Bharatas. The lord of the Madras, Shalya, is slain, and Shakuni, son of Subala, and Uluka, tiger among men, firm in valour, the Kaitavya.
Those creatures that roam by night barely stirred, and the creatures that range by day had come under sleep.
No dharma was honoured, saying always 'War'; all the kshatriyas have been destroyed and the fame of our foes increased.
Pritha, it is said, went to him, as we have heard: 'You are my son, and wish our welfare.'
[Janamejaya said:] "With this serpent dead, my child will not obtain life, hunter; I see no other benefit from killing him; therefore, hunter, release the serpent and let him live."
You ought not to follow the way of fools; adopt the way of your father and grandfather and bear the burden.
That bearer of the Kuru burden gave gifts to Brahmanas and the first fruits, and Kunti's son the king approved all of it.
From today, in all the houses of the Vrishnis and Andhakas here, no liquor or spirits are to be made by any of the citizens.
The great-souled Pandavas and the renowned Draupadi, O Kaurava, set out fasting from compassion, facing away.
Those great chariot-warriors who offered their bodies in the fire of battle, kings and princes who were slain in battle for my sake—
